analysis.note: Present active participial stem, from √dhyai/√dhyā; construed with puṃsaḥ and taking viṣayān as its accusative object.
Accusative object of dhyāyataḥ; rendered contextually as sense-objects.
Genitive singular; generic masculine rendered as “person.”
Refers back to viṣayān; in the printed saṃhitā teṣu + upajāyate appears as teṣūpajāyate.
Ātmanepada intransitive/kartari: “arises, comes into being”; printed in sandhi as part of teṣūpajāyate, with initial u coalesced.
Ātmanepada intransitive/kartari: “is born, arises”; avagraha in the printed text marks loss of initial a after krodho.

justifications.decision: With no commentary on this unit, the syntax is decided by agreement and government. dhyāyataḥ agrees with puṃsaḥ in masculine genitive singular, while viṣayān supplies the object of the mental act. The phrase is therefore rendered “for a person dwelling on the sense-objects,” not “from meditating.” The masculine puṃsaḥ is rendered generically as “person.”
options_considered: dhyāyataḥ as genitive singular participle qualifying puṃsaḥ, with viṣayān as object
justifications.chosen: dhyāyataḥ and puṃsaḥ as genitive singulars: “for/of a person contemplating”; viṣayān as the accusative object of the participle

justifications.decision: The dictionary range of viṣaya includes sphere/range, including the range of eyes, ears, mind, etc. In this psychological sequence of contemplation, attachment, desire, and anger, “sense-objects” is the appropriate contextual rendering, rather than “territories” or merely “topics.”

saṅga is construed with the locative teṣu, yielding “attachment to/in regard to them.” The ablatives saṅgāt and kāmāt mark the source or cause in the sequence: desire arises from attachment, anger from desire.
options_considered: attachment or clinging toward the objects
purely temporal ‘after attachment/desire’ rather than source-causal ablatives
justifications.chosen: saṅgaḥ teṣu = “attachment to them”; saṅgāt and kāmāt as source/causal ablatives

justifications.decision: The three ātmanepada finite verbs are read as intransitive kartari forms of √jan with prefixes upa, saṃ, and abhi. The translation therefore presents a causal arising, not a passive construction requiring an external agent: attachment arises, desire is born, anger is born.
options_considered: passive ‘is produced’ by an implied external maker
justifications.chosen: upajāyate, saṃjāyate, abhijāyate as intransitive kartari forms of √jan: “arises/is born”

one_shot_delta: No Śaṅkara-bhāṣya line is supplied for this unit, so there is no commentarial gloss to override the grammar. The main risk is grammatical: taking dhyāyataḥ as ablative “from meditating” rather than as a genitive participle qualifying puṃsaḥ.

A commentary-blind or context-blind rendering might translate viṣaya as “territories” or “domains” and saṅga as neutral “association,” missing the verse’s psychological chain: sense-object contemplation → attachment → desire → anger.
It might also treat the -jāyate verbs as passives with an implied agent, whereas the verse can be read straightforwardly as intransitive arising/becoming.
analyzer_disagreements: dhyāyataḥ: ByT5 gives the verbal lemma/root dhyā; here it is represented as the subanta present-participial stem dhyāyat, because the requested format asks for nominal stem plus case/gender/number for participles.

upajāyate, saṃjāyate, abhijāyate: ByT5 gives prefixed verbal lemmas upajan/saṃjan/abhijan; here these are decomposed into bare root jan plus prefixes upa/saṃ/abhi, per the required schema. The finite-verb features are otherwise retained.
mula: dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate | saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate
